# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–2 (Complete and Final – Updated 54)

## Setting and Time
- **Period**: Spring through late August of first year; Christmas/New Year period; nearly three weeks into new year (1832) just after Lords threw out Reform Bill; summer of first year; narrative extends into future years; present day with Fred and Mary at Stone Court in white-haired placidity
- **Primary Locations**: Middlemarch, Lowick, Grange, Freshitt, Mirecombe, Salwick, Quenwick, Fenmere, Bryngate, Chalky Flats, Gulton, Highbury, Cheltenham, Tipton, Yoddrell's farm, Frick, Miremere, Riverston, Quallingham, Halsell Wood, Loamford, Brassing, Stone Court, Coldcombe, St. Peter's Place, Lowick Gate, Shrubs, Dunholt, Yorkshire, Staveton, Bilkley, Harrowgate, Melspring, Wilhaven, Salford; Also: Chiswick Mall (Miss Pinkerton's academy location), England
- **Current Setting Details**: River crossing at Gulton; forge with chalked crooked sun on wall; wind from water with salt and tar smell; gulls quarreling over fish heads by steps; smoke from chimneys lying flat over fields; frost silvering hedges overnight; turnip cart passing well

## Main Characters

**Dorothea and Will Ladislaw (Married)**
- Engaged after Will's return to Middlemarch; Will had arms around her when she spoke of living on her seven-hundred-a-year fortune
- **Marriage**: Now married; has a little boy (infant); Celia expressed alarm that Will would hinder visits and concern about Dorothea's parenting and their fear she would die
- **Family Reconciliation**: Initial family opposition gradually resolved; Mr. Brooke corresponded with Will and Dorothea, sent invitation to Grange during months of correspondence while presupposing to Sir James Chettam that entail-cutting intention maintained; Mr. Brooke conveyed stronger sense than ever of reasons for energetic step against low blood mixture in Brooke heir
- **Visits to Family**: Established pattern of at least two visits yearly to Grange; Dorothea and Will's cousins at Freshitt enjoyed playing with their two cousins visiting Tipton as much as if blood less dubiously mixed
- **Sir James's Enduring Opposition**: Never ceased regarding second marriage as mistake; became tradition in Middlemarch that she married sickly clergyman old enough to be father, then within year gave up estate to marry his cousin—young, propertyless, not well-born; those unfamiliar with Dorothea usually observed she could not have been "nice woman" else would not have married either
- **Will's Relationship with Sir James**: Never liked each other; on footing of reciprocal tolerance made easy only when Dorothea and Celia present; Sir James preferred company mixed with other kind
- **Dorothea's Life Assessment**: Acts not ideally beautiful but mixed result of young, noble impulse struggling amidst imperfect social conditions where great feelings take aspect of error and faith takes aspect of illusion; finely touched spirit had fine issues though not widely visible; full nature spent itself in channels with no great name on earth; effect of her being on those around her incalculably diffusive; growing good of world partly dependent on unhistoric acts; that things not so ill with others half owing to those who lived faithfully hidden life and rest in unvisited tombs

**Mary Garth and Fred Garth (Married)**
- **Present Status**: Still inhabit Stone Court; creeping plants cast foam of blossoms over fine stone-wall into field where walnut-trees stand in stately row; on sunny days seen in white-haired placidity at open window from which Mary once had been ordered to look out for Mr. Lydgate in old Peter Featherstone's days
- **Marriage Achievement**: Solid mutual happiness; Fred makes no failure; becomes rather distinguished in county as theoretic and practical farmer; produces work on "Cultivation of Green Crops and the Economy of Cattle-Feeding" winning high congratulations at agricultural meetings; Middlemarch admiration more reserved—most inclined to believe merit due to Mary since never expected Fred Vincy to write on turnips and mangel-wurzel
- **Fred's Character Development**: Remains unswervingly steady some years after marriage; told Mary happiness half owing to Farebrother who gave strong pull-up at right moment; never wholly free from misled hopefulness—crop yields and profits usually fell below estimate; always prone to believe could make money by horse purchase which turned out badly; Mary observed fault of horse, not Fred's judgment; kept love of horsemanship but rarely allowed hunting days; when did hunt, remarkable he submitted to being laughed at for cowardliness at fences, seeming to see Mary and boys sitting on five-barred gate or showing curly heads between hedge and ditch; gradually saved enough to become owner of stock and furniture at Stone Court; work Garth put in his hands carried him through always-present "bad times" with farmers
- **Fred's Feelings**: Had pleasant vision on winter evenings of bright hearth in wainscoted parlor; sorry for other men who could not have Mary for wife, especially Mr. Farebrother; told Mary magnanimously "He was ten times worthier of you than I was"; Mary answered "To be sure he was, and for that reason he could do better without me. But you—I shudder to think what you would have been—a curate in debt for horse-hire and cambric pocket-handkerchiefs!"
- **Children**: Three boys only, not discontented; youngest very much what her father must have been when wore round jacket, showed marvellous nicety of aim in marbles and throwing stones for pears; Mary brings forth little formal teaching, alarming Mrs. Garth lest never well grounded in grammar and geography; nevertheless children found quite forward when went to school, perhaps because liked nothing so well as being with mother

**Lydgate and Rosamond**: Made final resolution to leave Middlemarch; Dorothea sent letter with check for thousand pounds; Lydgate has accepted narrowed lot with sad resignation; full of timid care for wife; Rosamond meek enough to nestle under old despised shelter; has sent daughters away to board at school on coast that crisis might be hidden; pride broken down between two women

**Caleb Garth**: Had tender concern for Mary's contentment; expresses belief woman must not force her heart; voice shook perceptibly when speaking of Fred and Mary's marriage

**New Middlemarch Characters**
- **Nynelle Stenworth**: A woman living in Gulton; mended torn sleeve by window and said little; married Halan Hollwood; gave birth to son Rozek Hollwood; lived in Gulton with family
- **Orbin Stenworth**: Male character in Middlemarch; complained of aching back as usual; mended torn sleeve by window and said little; told Orrine Stenworth "You look tired," and Orrine did not deny it
- **Orrine Stenworth**: Female character; bought a ribbon at the stall and then regretted it; told by Orbin Stenworth "You look tired," and did not deny it
- **Halan Hollwood**: Married Nynelle Stenworth; father of Rozek Hollwood; said "The price of salt is a scandal" with Rozek agreeing
- **Rozek Hollwood**: Son born to Nynelle Stenworth and Halan Hollwood; family lived in Gulton; argued with carter over price of sack of oats; said "A scandal" in response to Halan about salt price

## Family Reactions

**Sir James Chettam**: Still in white indignation initially; said if Ladislaw had spark of honor would have gone out of country; said not surprised, emphasized delicacy ought to have forbidden seeing him again; listed grievances: takes her from proper rank into poverty, accepts such sacrifice, objectionable position, bad origin, man of little principle; unable to take Ladislaw into family; acknowledged to himself jealous repugnance not entirely different from reaction to Casaubon; acknowledges marriage fatal for Dorothea; motivated by undeniable fact that union of estates—Tipton and Freshitt—flattered him for son and heir; felt sudden embarrassment when Mr. Brooke mentioned cutting off entail; Eventually consented to reconciliation—inevitably where women love each other, men smother mutual dislike; never liked Ladislaw; never ceased regarding marriage as mistake

**Celia Chettam**: Said very bad, you have disappointed us all; expressed disbelief marriage "ever will be"; blamed them for doing nothing to hinder it; later expressed wish for reconciliation, saying Dorothea has little boy, that Will hinders her from visiting, that Dorothea wants to see her, that they thought she would die, expressing it very dreadful; wished James would be less unkind

**Mr. Brooke**: Tried to dissuade initially, pointed out poverty and abandoning position; she quite determined; came to Lowick after she sent for him; it came about quite suddenly; did his duty but she acts as she likes; can cut off entail but will cost money and be troublesome; could not resist pleasure of corresponding with Will and Dorothea; one morning pen fluent on Municipal Reform prospects ran off into invitation to Grange which once written could not be done away with; during months of correspondence continually presupposed or hinted to Sir James that entail-cutting intention maintained; day invitation given, went to Freshitt expressly to intimate stronger sense than ever of reasons for energetic step as precaution against low blood mixture in heir; later meeting Sir James in grounds, began to chat in ignorance of news; when entail touched on, said "My dear sir, it is not for me to dictate to you, but for my part I would let that alone. I would let things remain as they are."

**Mr. and Mrs. Cadwallader**: Should not condemn as wrong because men have poor opinion of each other; apt to consider act wrong because unpleasant to them; said should not make fuss if she likes to be poor that is her affair; nobody would have said anything if married young fellow because he was rich; noted plenty of beneficed clergy poorer than they will be; had hardly thousand a-year himself, was lout, nobody saw anything in him; must take Ladislaw's part until hearing more harm; Mrs. Cadwallader said "there is usually a silent exception in such cases," only wonder any surprised, blamed them for doing nothing to hinder it, blamed Mr. Casaubon for preparing it all beautifully by making himself disagreeable

## Bulstrode Family Matters

**Mr. Bulstrode**: Told wife (Harriet) intends not to sell land in neighborhood but leave it to her as safe provision; discussed making amends to Rosamond and her husband; mentioned Garth once thought of undertaking management of Stone Court; stock to remain as is, they to pay certain share of profits instead of ordinary rent; suggested desirable beginning for young man in conjunction with employment under Garth; told Harriet she must make proposal to Garth herself; can put into her hands paper Garth himself drew up, stating conditions; she can propose his renewed acceptance

**Harriet Bulstrode**: Expressed wish to do something for brother's family (Fred and Mary Garth); thinks bound to make amends to Rosamond and her husband; mentioned Walter says Mr. Lydgate must leave town; seemed cut severely by Mrs. Casaubon's check; tears fell one after other, chin trembling; Bulstrode ached at sight of grief-worn face which two months before had been bright and blooming; aged to keep sad company with his withered features

## Earlier Rumors and Unverified Claims Preserved
- Wife of Ridan Corrett confided to Ilzek Wexwood that bridge toll at Salwick skimmed every month
- Gossip claimed Thidrek Corrett and Rira Stenworth had been wed in secret
- Cotho Hollwood quit Wilhaven after quarrel, took lodgings in Coldcombe
- Lindson blood debt to Hollmere; Lindson mill ledger rewritten after flood; Salford granary fire set on purpose; old abbey at Salford second cellar; Bryngate pastures deed forged; silver chest buried beneath Mirecombe well; Quenwick chapel vault opens only for living person with jade ring and oak comb; Dunholt toll bridge belonged to Wexwood family
